SOURCE: "Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP", Neil Houlsby, Andrei Giurgiu, Stanisław Jastrzębski, Bruna Morrone, Quentin de Laroussilhe, Andrea Gesmundo, Mona Attariyan, Sylvain Gelly (Google Research; Jagiellonian University). Venue as printed: "Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, Long Beach, California, PMLR 97, 2019" (ICML 2019). arXiv:1902.00751v2, 13 Jun 2019.

COVERAGE: I read all 52,264 of 52,264 extracted characters. That covers every page: the main text, the references, and the appendices (Tables 3 to 7, App. B, Fig. 7). I skimmed the references for origins only. The AutoML search-space tables (5 to 7) are only baseline configuration, so I just noted them. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/08-multimodal-engineering/sources/houlsby-2019-parameter-efficient-transfer-learning-nlp.pdf

CLAIMS
- claim: On GLUE, adapter tuning of BERT-large scores within 0.4 of full fine-tuning while training 3.6% of the parameters per task.
  number: 80.0 vs 80.4 mean GLUE; 3.6% trained params per task; 1.3x vs 9.0x total params
  setup: BERT-LARGE (24 layers, 330M params). Scored on GLUE test sets via the evaluation server, WNLI omitted. Adapter size picked per task from {8, 64, 256}. LR swept over {3e-5, 3e-4, 3e-3}, epochs over {3, 20}. Best of 5 seeds, picked on validation "due to training instability". MNLI-m and MNLI-mm treated as separate tasks.
  quote: "On GLUE, we attain within 0.4% of the performance of full ﬁne-tuning, adding only 3.6% parameters per task." / "Adapters achieve a mean GLUE score of 80.0, compared to 80.4 achieved by full ﬁne-tuning." / Table 1: "BERTLARGE 9.0× 100% ... 80.4", "Adapters (8-256) 1.3× 3.6% ... 80.0"
  where: abstract p1; Sec 3.2 p4; Table 1 p5
- claim: If the adapter size is fixed at 64 for every task, the GLUE score drops slightly and the model gets slightly smaller.
  number: 79.6; 2.1% params/task; 1.2x total
  setup: same as the row above, with size 64 for all tasks
  quote: "Restricting always to size 64, leads to a small decrease in average accuracy to 79.6." / "Adapters (64) 1.2× 2.1% ... 79.6"
  where: Sec 3.2 p4; Table 1 p5
- claim: At a similar trainable-parameter budget, adapters clearly beat fine-tuning only the top layer.
  number: top layer about 9M params, 77.8% MNLI-m; adapters size 64 about 2M params, 83.7%; full fine-tune 84.4%
  setup: BERT-BASE, MNLI-m validation accuracy, ±1 s.e.m. over 3 seeds
  quote: "ﬁne-tuning just the top layer yields approximately 9M train-able parameters and 77.8%± 0.1% validation accuracy on MNLIm. In contrast, adapter tuning with size 64 yields ap-proximately 2M trainable parameters and 83.7%± 0.1% validation accuracy. For comparison, full ﬁne-tuning attains 84.4%± 0.02% on MNLIm."
  where: Sec 3.4 p5
- claim: Across task suites, adapters stay close to full fine-tuning while training about two orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Fine-tuning the top layers degrades sharply on GLUE as fewer layers are trained.
  number: "two orders of magnitude"
  setup: Figs 1 and 3. Scores are normalized by full fine-tuning, with 20/50/80th percentiles across tasks. GLUE uses BERT-LARGE and validation accuracy; the additional tasks use BERT-BASE and test accuracy.
  quote: "Adapter-based tuning attains a similar performance to full ﬁne-tuning with two orders of magnitude fewer trained parameters." / "On GLUE, performance decreases dra-matically when fewer layers are ﬁne-tuned."
  where: Fig 1 caption p1; Sec 3.4 p5
- claim: On 17 additional classification tasks, adapters are 0.4 behind full fine-tuning at 1.14% params per task. Variable fine-tuning (top n layers) does slightly better but trains about half the network.
  number: avg 73.3 adapters, 73.7 fine-tune, 74.0 variable FT, 72.7 AutoML; totals 1.19x, 17x, 9.9x; trained per task 1.14%, 100%, 52.9%
  setup: BERT-BASE. Adapter sizes {2..64}, n in {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12}. Test accuracy with s.e.m. over seeds. Datasets range from 900 to 330k training examples and 2 to 157 classes.
  quote: "The performance of adapter-tuning is close to full ﬁne-tuning (0.4% behind)." / "They intro-duce 1.14% new parameters per task, resulting in 1.19× parameters for all 17 tasks." / "Average 72.7 73 .7 74 .0 73 .3"
  where: Sec 3.3 p4; Table 2 p5
- claim: Adapter architecture: a bottleneck (down-project d to m, nonlinearity, up-project to d) with an internal skip connection. It is inserted twice per Transformer layer, after the attention projection and after the FFN, before the residual add and the LayerNorm. Each task trains the adapters, new LayerNorm parameters, and the classifier head.
  number: 2md + d + m params per layer; 0.5 to 8% of the model in practice
  setup: standard Transformer (Vaswani 2017) as used in BERT
  quote: "The total number of parameters added per layer, including biases, is 2md +d +m. By setting m≪ d, we limit the number of parameters added per task; in practice, we use around 0.5− 8% of the parameters of the original model."

- claim: Near-identity initialization is needed for stable training. Weights are drawn from a truncated Gaussian with std 1e-2, and performance is robust below that but degrades when the init is too large, more so on CoLA.

LIMITS:
- Only text classification and extractive QA are tested, on BERT-base and BERT-large encoders. There is no generation, no decoder LLM, and no vision or multimodal model. Anything said about VLMs is extrapolation.
- The method costs inference latency, because it adds serial layers, but the paper never measures that. It reports no training-time or memory savings either; the only efficiency metric is stored parameters per task.
- GLUE results take the best of 5 seeds, re-run "due to training instability", so the variance is understated.
- The paper does not specify which nonlinearity the bottleneck uses.
- The ablations of the complex variants give no numbers or datasets.
- The LR robustness figure (App. B, Fig 7) has no stated conclusion in the text.
- The paper is internally inconsistent. It says "3%" (intro, Sec 3) where the abstract and Table 1 say 3.6%, and "52%" in the text where Table 2 says 52.9%. "Within 0.4%" is really 0.4 GLUE points (80.4 vs 80.0).
- Dated: there is no comparison with LoRA or prefix-tuning, which came later.
- Concurrent work (PALs, Stickland & Murray 2019) is mentioned but not compared head to head.

BUILDS ON: residual adapters in vision (Rebuffi et al., 2017; 2018; Rosenfeld & Tsotsos, 2018), which use 1x1 conv adapters at about 11% growth per task. It also credits BERT (Devlin et al., 2018), Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), and conditional BN, FiLM and self-modulation for the LayerNorm tuning (De Vries et al., 2017; Perez et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019). It cites the top-layer focus of ULMFiT (Howard & Ruder, 2018), catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey & Cohen, 1989; French, 1999), and Neural AutoML (Zoph & Le, 2017; Wong et al., 2018) for the baseline.

CODE: none in the paper. It gives only a link: "Code at https://github.com/google-research/adapter-bert" (footnote 1, p1).

FIGURES:
- Fig 2 (p3): "Architecture of the adapter module and its integration with the Transformer." This is the clearest picture of placement (twice per layer) and of the bottleneck with its skip connection. Best single figure for the note.
- Fig 1 (p1) / Fig 3 (p6): accuracy delta vs trainable params per task, adapters vs fine-tuning the top layers. Shows the two-orders-of-magnitude gap at a glance.
- Fig 4 (p6): MNLI-m and CoLA validation accuracy vs params for adapters, top-k fine-tuning and LayerNorm-only. Shows all three PEFT choices on one axis.
- Fig 6 (p8): layer-span removal heatmaps plus the init-scale sweep. Shows that higher layers matter more and that near-identity init is needed.
- Fig 5 (p7) SQuAD trade-off and Fig 7 (p13) LR robustness are less essential.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean apart from minor spacing artifacts in the tables (e.g. "94 .9") and ligatures. There were no embedded instructions.
